executive_summary: August 2026 presents a striking split in investor psychology: both institutional and individual investors express strong confidence that markets will recover quickly from any pullback, yet neither group feels particularly safe from a crash. Crash worries actually deepened compared to July, even as buy-on-dips confidence surged to its highest recorded levels in recent months. It's a bit like fastening your seatbelt while flooring the accelerator — investors seem to believe turbulence is possible but recoverable.

key_findings.headline: Institutions Bounce Back Sharply
key_findings.interpretation: Institutional 1-Year Confidence jumped back to 85.71% after dipping to 66.67% in July, while individual confidence slipped from 80.0% to 72.22%. This could reflect institutions reacting to new data or simply reverting to a longer-term optimistic baseline, while individuals may be responding to different signals or risk tolerances.

key_findings.headline: Crash Fears Quietly Intensify
key_findings.interpretation: Only 30% of institutional investors and 22% of individuals feel confident a crash won't happen in the next six months — both down from July's already modest readings. This suggests that a meaningful majority in both groups view a crash as at least plausible, though whether that reflects specific risks or general unease is hard to say from the numbers alone.

key_findings.headline: Dip-Buying Faith Soars
key_findings.interpretation: Every single institutional respondent — 100% — believes a sharp one-day drop would fully recover within two days, and 87.5% of individuals agree. This remarkable surge from July's 45% range may suggest investors see the market as having strong underlying demand, or it could reflect recency bias from quick recoveries in prior selloffs.

key_findings.headline: Valuation Views Still Divided
key_findings.interpretation: Two-thirds of institutional investors don't consider the market overvalued, up from 60% in July, while individual confidence held steady at 40%. It's worth noting that some institutional investors subscribe to efficient-market theory, where asking about overvaluation is essentially a non-question — the price is, by definition, the right price.

detailed_analysis:
The most eye-catching number this month is the buy-on-dips reading. Institutional confidence hit a perfect 100%, and individuals weren't far behind at 87.5%. That's a dramatic reversal from July, when both groups hovered around 45%. One reading of this: investors may have recently watched the market snap back from a pullback, reinforcing a "buy every dip" reflex. Another possibility is that expectations for policy support — monetary or otherwise — are giving investors comfort that selloffs will be short-lived.

But here's the tension. Even as both groups express near-total faith in quick recoveries, crash worries are actually getting worse. Institutional crash confidence fell to 30% and individual crash confidence to just 22%. In plain terms, most investors think a crash is a real possibility — they just also believe the market would bounce right back. Whether those two beliefs can coexist comfortably for long is an open question.

The 1-Year Confidence numbers tell a familiar story of institutional and individual investors marching to different drums. Institutions swung from 67% in July back up to 86% in August, nearly matching their June level. Individuals moved the other way, easing from 80% to 72%. These kinds of month-to-month reversals may simply reflect the different information flows and decision-making horizons of the two groups rather than any deep disagreement about fundamentals.

Valuation confidence inched higher among institutions (to 67%) while holding flat for individuals (40%). The persistent gap here is worth noting: individual investors are far more likely to feel the market is expensive. Whether that's a sign of healthy skepticism or excessive caution depends on your perspective — and, as noted, some professionals would argue the question itself is moot if you believe markets are efficient.
methodology: These indices come from the Yale/Shiller U.S. Stock Market Confidence Surveys, which have tracked investor sentiment since 1989. Each month, roughly 100 wealthy individual investors and 100 institutional investment managers answer the same standardized questions. The consistency of those questions over 35+ years is what makes the data meaningful — you can actually compare investor psychology across very different market environments. The four indices each measure something distinct: • 1-Year Confidence: The share who expect prices to be higher in 12 months. • Crash Confidence: The share who believe a crash in the next 6 months is very unlikely (under 10% probability). A low reading means most people think a crash is plausible. • Buy-on-Dips Confidence: The share who believe that after a 3% single-day market drop, prices would fully recover within two days. • Valuation Confidence: The share who do not believe the market is overvalued. Surveys were conducted semi-annually before 2001 and have been monthly since July 2001. Respondents rotate over time, but consistent characteristics — high income, investment experience — are maintained across the panel.
